lesson.title: A Manageable Slice: Understanding Samples
lesson.summary: This section defines a sample as a subset of a population that is actually measured, explains why researchers use samples instead of censuses, and works through estimating a population characteristic from a small sample of Lincoln High students.
lesson.body:
The previous section defined a population as the complete group a researcher ultimately wants to learn about, using Lincoln High School's 1,200 students as an example. A sample is a subset of that population, a smaller group actually selected and measured, used to learn something about the much larger population it was drawn from. Researchers use samples instead of full censuses for practical reasons: surveying, measuring, or testing every single member of a large population is often too expensive, too slow, or logistically impossible, while a well chosen sample can often deliver a very good estimate at a fraction of the cost.

The phrase "well chosen" is doing a lot of work in that last sentence, and it points to the central challenge of sampling. A sample is only useful to the extent that it actually represents the population it came from. If a researcher wants to know the sleep habits of all 1,200 Lincoln High students but only surveys members of the varsity swim team, who might keep unusually disciplined schedules, the resulting sample would likely give a misleading picture of the whole school. This is why statisticians favor random sampling, where every member of the population has a known chance of being selected, specifically because it avoids systematically favoring any particular subgroup and tends to produce a sample that looks like a smaller version of the full population.

Consider a worked example that continues directly from the population section. Suppose a researcher cannot survey all 1,200 Lincoln High students about their sleep habits, and instead selects a random sample of just 10 students. Their reported hours of sleep on a typical school night are: 7, 6, 8, 7, 5, 9, 6, 7, 8, and 7 hours. Adding these 10 values gives 7 + 6 + 8 + 7 + 5 + 9 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 7 = 70. Dividing that sum by the 10 students in the sample gives a sample average of 70 divided by 10, which equals exactly 7.0 hours. Unlike the population proportion calculated in the previous section, this sample average of 7.0 hours is not necessarily the exact truth about all 1,200 students. It is an estimate, based on only 10 of them, and a different random sample of 10 different students would likely produce a slightly different average, perhaps 6.8 hours or 7.3 hours, simply due to which particular students happened to be selected.

This gap between what a sample tells you and what is actually true of the full population is called sampling variability, and it is one of the central ideas in all of statistics. A larger, well selected sample generally gives a more reliable estimate than a smaller one, but even a large random sample will almost never match the population exactly. Statisticians have developed careful tools for quantifying exactly how much a sample based estimate can be trusted, but the starting point for all of that work is simply recognizing that a sample is a partial, imperfect stand in for the full population, not the population itself.

Numbers calculated from an entire population, like the 52.1 percent female proportion computed in the previous section, and numbers calculated from a sample, like the 7.0 hour average calculated here, are given different names in statistics specifically because one is exact and the other is an estimate. The next section introduces the term for the population version of these numbers: the parameter.
